cards.subject: history

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.front: Name the grains found at Harappan sites.

wheat
barley
lentil
chickpea
sesame

cards.front: Name the animals whose bones are found at Harappan sites.
cards.back:
cattle
sheep
goat
buffalo
pig

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.front: What did Cunningham note in 1875 about brick taken from Harappa?
cards.back: As early as 1875, Alexander Cunningham, the first Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI), often called the father of Indian archaeology, noted that the amount of brick taken from the ancient site was enough to lay bricks for "about 100 miles" of the railway line between Lahore and Multan.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

reasons: review:Tests the 100-mile railway-brick anecdote, which is case-story trivia; the examinable points (first Director-General, father of Indian archaeology) are not what the front asks.

cards.subject: history
cards.front: What was one of the most distinctive features of Harappan cities?

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history

cards.subject: history
cards.front: Utilitarian objects vs luxuries: how do archaeologists tell them apart?
cards.back: The first category includes objects of daily use made fairly easily out of ordinary materials such as stone or clay. These include querns, pottery, needles, flesh-rubbers (body scrubbers), etc., and are usually found distributed throughout settlements. Archaeologists assume objects were luxuries if they are rare or made from costly, non-local materials or with complicated technologies.
cards.quote: The first category includes objects of daily use made fairly easily out of ordinary materials such as stone or clay. These include querns, pottery, needles, flesh-rubbers (body scrubbers), etc., and are usually found distributed throughout settlements. Archaeologists assume objects were luxuries if they are rare or made from costly, non-local materials or with complicated technologies.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

reasons: review:Back begins 'The first category' and never names utilitarian objects, so it does not stand alone as a utilitarian-vs-luxury difference.

cards.subject: history

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.subject: history
cards.front: Two views of archaeologists on rulers in Harappan society (no rulers; several rulers).
cards.back:
Some archaeologists are of the opinion that Harappan society had no rulers, and that everybody enjoyed equal status.
Others feel there was no single ruler but several, that Mohenjodaro had a separate ruler, Harappa another, and so forth.
cards.quote: Some archaeologists are of the opinion that Harappan society had no rulers, and that everybody enjoyed equal status. Others feel there was no single ruler but several, that Mohenjodaro had a separate ruler, Harappa another, and so forth.

source.book: Themes in Indian History Part I

cards.note: A third view in NCERT: a single state, given the similarity in artefacts and planned settlements.
reasons: review:Front states 'no rulers; several rulers' (gives the answer away) and says 'two views', but NCERT gives three (the third: a single state); the types card is incomplete.

cards.subject: history
cards.front: Major periods in early Indian archaeology, in order, with dates.
cards.back:
2 million BP Lower Palaeolithic
80,000 Middle Palaeolithic
35,000 Upper Palaeolithic
12,000 Mesolithic
10,000 Neolithic (early agriculturists and pastoralists)
6,000 Chalcolithic (first use of copper)
2600 BCE Harappan civilisation
1000 BCE Early iron, megalithic burials
600 BCE-400 CE Early Historic
cards.quote: 2 million BP Lower Palaeolithic (BEFORE PRESENT) 80,000 Middle Palaeolithic 35,000 Upper Palaeolithic 12,000 Mesolithic 10,000 Neolithic (early agriculturists and pastoralists) 6,000 Chalcolithic (first use of copper) 2600 BCE Harappan civilisation 1000 BCE Early iron, megalithic burials 600 BCE-400 CE Early Historic
